question: According to media reports, a non-EU entity is set to launch the television channel Newsmax Polska in Poland. The Serbian public company Telekom Srbija is overseeing the process as a co-owner. Notably, the media has highlighted that the Serbian company was previously cofinanced by the Russian bank Sberbank.

Media freedom in Serbia has further deteriorated, as evidenced by its fall to 98th place in Reporters Without Borders’ 2024 World Press Freedom Index. Reports adopted by Parliament indicate that Serbia must improve media diversity and pluralism, and highlight numerous concerns regarding media freedom in the country. 1.

Given that media freedom and pluralism are enshrined in the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union and that legal tools are available under the European Media Freedom Act, what actions will the Commission take to prevent Russian interference in Member States?
Will the Commission monitor the situation and take action if media freedom is threatened?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (23.6.2026) The freedom and pluralism of the media are enshrined in Article 11 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union, and the Commission is committed to ensuring its respect within the remit of its competences.

In the context of Russia’s illegal war of aggression against Ukraine, the EU has imposed restrictive measures (sanctions) on Russian media outlets because of their role in supporting and justifying this war of aggression and disseminating Russian disinformation.

Currently, 32 media outlets are subject to a broadcasting ban and have had their EU broadcasting licenses suspended, having been included in Annex XV to Regulation (EU) 833/20141 and Annex IX to Decision 2014/512/CFSP2. It is therefore prohibited to disseminate any content from these media outlets in the EU. The implementation and enforcement of EU sanctions are primarily the responsibility of the Member States.

In its role as guardian of the Treaties, the Commission oversees the implementation and enforcement of EU sanctions across Member States. Moreover, the European Media Freedom Act3 allows for swift and efficient coordination of actions against rogue non-EU media service providers presenting risks to public security, entrusted to EU media regulators, gathered in the European Board for Media Services4.
The Commission also continues to monitor specific developments regarding media independence and pluralism in the Member States and in four enlargement countries5 as part of the Rule of Law Report.
1 Council Regulation (EU) No 833/2014 of 31 July 2014 concerning restrictive measures in view of Russia's

actions destabilising the situation in Ukraine, OJ L 229, 31.7.2014, pp. 1–11. 2 Council Decision 2014/512/CFSP of 31 July 2014 concerning restrictive measures in view of Russia's actions destabilising the situation in Ukraine, OJ L 229, 31.7.2014, pp. 13–17.

3 Regulation (EU) 2024/1083 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 11 April 2024 establishing a common framework for media services in the internal market and amending Directive 2010/13/EU (European Media Freedom Act), OJ L, 2024/1083, 17.4.2024. 4 Article 17 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1083. 5 Montenegro, Albania, North Macedonia and Serbia.
